interviewQuestions.question: What does "secure by default" mean, and why does it matter more than writing good documentation about the safe way to use something?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It means whatever a user does with the least effort — leaving a setting alone, calling a function with no extra arguments — should be the safest available behavior, not the most permissive one. The reasoning is about how software actually gets built: most developers under a real deadline take the default and move on, they don't read every configuration option or every security advisory.

That's exactly why documentation is a weaker lever than a default. A security note saying "remember to enable X" reaches whoever happens to read the docs, and only helps if they act on it before shipping — anyone who joined the project after the note was written may never see it. Changing the actual default reaches every single user of that library or framework automatically, the next time they update the dependency, with zero effort or awareness required on their part.

A concrete example I'd give: a templating engine that auto-escapes output by default doesn't just make the safe choice easy, it removes an entire class of "forgot to escape user input" XSS bugs for every developer who uses the standard mechanism, retroactively, the moment the framework itself does it right — versus asking every individual call site to remember to escape correctly, forever.

**Testing:** whether you understand secure-by-default as a leverage argument about developer behavior at scale, not just a nice-to-have engineering practice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between fail-safe and fail-open, and how do you decide which one is correct for a given check?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is about what happens when a check *can't run at all* — the dependency it needs is down, it throws an exception, it times out — which is a genuinely different question from what happens when the check runs and returns "no." Fail-safe (fail-closed) treats an unevaluated check as a denial; fail-open treats it as permission granted, letting the request through anyway.

The decision comes down to classifying what the check actually protects. For authentication, authorization, and payment validation, fail-safe is almost always correct — an incorrect "allow" there is a direct security failure, and the cost of fail-safe is availability impact (legitimate requests blocked while something's broken), which is the lesser evil. For checks that protect availability or UX rather than security — a personalization service being down, in some designs a rate limiter's own backing infrastructure failing — fail-open can be the deliberate, defensible choice, because the alternative (the check's own outage taking the whole service down) is judged worse than temporarily skipping a non-security feature.

The trap is that fail-open on a security-relevant check is almost never a deliberate decision — it's usually an accident, typically a bare try/catch around a permission check written by someone thinking only about preventing a crash, not about what the fallback behavior actually grants. I audit for this specifically by tracing every exit path of a security check, not just the pass/fail branches, but the throws-an-exception and times-out branches too.

**Testing:** whether you can classify a given check correctly and articulate the trade-off, rather than reciting 'always fail-safe' as an absolute rule that doesn't actually hold universally.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: You're reviewing a pull request that wraps a new authorization check in a try/catch to handle a flaky downstream permission service. What would you look for, and what would you push back on?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The first thing I'd check is exactly what the catch block does — not whether it exists, but its actual behavior on the error path. If it sets the permission result to "allowed" or lets execution fall through to code that assumes the check passed, that's an accidental fail-open on a security-relevant check, and I'd push back on it directly regardless of how reasonable the crash-prevention intent was, because the fix for a flaky dependency shouldn't come at the cost of an authorization bypass during every outage of that dependency.

The correct default I'd ask for is denying the request on any error evaluating the check — timeout, exception, unreachable service — the same fail-safe posture as an explicit "no" from the check itself. If the team has a real availability concern (this permission service being flaky enough that fail-safe would cause frequent unwanted denials), that's a legitimate conversation to have, but it needs to happen explicitly, with the security trade-off named and reviewed, not decided implicitly by whatever the try/catch happened to default to.

I'd also ask whether this is the only place in the codebase with this pattern, because a permission check written to handle a specific flaky dependency is exactly the kind of code that gets copy-pasted into other checks later — worth flagging as a pattern to search for elsewhere, not just fixing in this one PR.

**Testing:** whether you can review code for exactly this failure mode in a realistic PR-review scenario, not just discuss the concept abstractly.

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer, how would you push a platform team to adopt secure defaults more broadly, beyond fixing individual known issues as they're found?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as a leverage argument, because that's what actually gets platform investment prioritized: fixing one instance of an insecure default helps one team, but changing the default itself in a shared library, framework, or platform template helps every current and future consumer of it automatically, with no additional effort from any of them. That ratio — one fix, many beneficiaries, indefinitely — is exactly the kind of investment a platform team should be optimizing for over one-off remediations.

Concretely, I'd audit the platform's shared building blocks — the internal service template every new microservice starts from, the shared HTTP client library, the standard database access layer — for opt-in-to-secure patterns (CSRF protection, parameterized queries, TLS verification, auth checks) and flip them to opt-out-to-disable wherever feasible, since that's the pattern that reaches every consumer without asking them to remember anything.

For the harder cases — an existing insecure default that many services already depend on and would break if flipped immediately — I'd push for the same staged rollout used elsewhere in this area: introduce the new secure default behind a flag, default it on for new services immediately, and give existing services a migration path and deadline rather than either flipping it silently (risking an outage) or leaving the insecure default in place indefinitely because migrating everyone at once feels too risky to start.

The cultural piece I'd also push: treating 'we shipped a secure default' as a bigger win in review and planning than 'we fixed this one team's misconfiguration,' since that's what gets the org actually optimizing for the higher-leverage work instead of always reacting to individual findings.

**Testing:** whether you can make the organizational case for platform-level investment, not just the technical case for any individual default.
